newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian president vows more anti-rebel efforts.
newsitem.headline: Colombian president vows more anti-rebel efforts.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper on Monday vowed stepped up counterinsurgency measures as a 10-day-old rebel offensive continued claiming lives across Colombia.
At least nine guerrillas and one soldier died in various parts of the country over the weekend -- taking the total death toll to more than 120 mostly soldiers and police since Aug. 30.
In an interview with El Tiempo, Colombia's leading daily, Samper promised military intelligence would be stepped up, communication links boosted and troop mobility by land, air and river improved.

"The government is aware of the seriousness of the situation but at this time we are in control of the situation despite all the difficulties. We have suffered casualties but so have the guerrillas," he said.
Despite the wave of recent attacks, the president insisted the situation was under control.

Two rebels from the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second guerrilla force, died in the eastern province of Arauca in a failed attempt to dynamite the Cano Limon-Covenas oil pipeline over the weekend, military sources said.

A separate attack on Saturday on the Transandean pipeline in the south was successful, however. The state oil company, Ecopetrol, said 1,500 barrels of crude were lost and operations were suspended until Monday.

Four more ELN rebels died in firefights with the military in the northern province of Magdalena and Antioquia in the northwest, and an army spokesman said two guerrillas from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's largest and oldest insurgent force, had been killed in northeastern Santander province.

In southern Putumayo province, site of some of the worst fighting in more than three decades of guerrilla war, Gov. Jorge Fuerbringer said the FARC was virtually laying siege to the capital, Mocoa. FARC rebels overran a military base in the remote Las Delicias area of Putumayo on Aug. 30, killing more than 30 soldiers and kidnapping 67.

In a communique sent to the International Red Cross early on Monday rebel leaders denied any of the captive soliders had been tortured. The rebels have said they will only free the soldiers if the release zone is demilitarized three days before, and they have called for international representatives to witness the handover.
One of the major problems said to be facing the Colombian military is its lack of mobility. The army only has about 35 helicopters to transport ground troops to conflict zones.
